passages.title: How Vietnam Became the World's Second-Largest Coffee Producer
passages.passage:
Most coffee drinkers in Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City would tell you that coffee is part of daily life. What many do not realize is that Vietnam produces more coffee than any country except Brazil. The story of how Vietnam reached this position is short but remarkable.

Coffee was first introduced to Vietnam by French missionaries in the mid-nineteenth century. For more than a hundred years, production remained modest, concentrated in small plots in the Central Highlands. After the country opened its economy in the late 1980s, the government encouraged farmers to plant coffee on a large scale. Within two decades, Vietnam transformed from a minor producer into a global powerhouse, with exports growing more than fifty times.

The coffee grown in Vietnam is mostly Robusta, a variety known for its strong, bitter taste and high caffeine content. While Arabica beans dominate specialty cafes in Western countries, Robusta is preferred for instant coffee blends and is widely used by global brands that need a consistent supply at a reasonable price. This focus on Robusta is one reason Vietnamese coffee is sometimes overlooked by foreign critics, but it is also why the country has been so successful commercially.

In recent years, a new generation of Vietnamese roasters has begun to challenge the old image. Small companies in Da Lat and Buon Ma Thuot are experimenting with Arabica beans and refined processing techniques. Their goal is not to replace Robusta, but to show that Vietnam can produce high-quality specialty coffee as well. International competitions have already started to recognize beans from these regions.

The future of Vietnamese coffee will depend on several factors. Climate change threatens traditional growing areas, and younger farmers are leaving the countryside for jobs in the city. At the same time, the global appetite for coffee continues to grow, and Vietnam has the experience and infrastructure to remain a leading supplier. Whether the country becomes known for quantity, quality, or both, coffee will almost certainly continue to be a defining part of its economy and identity.

passages.title: The Rise of Remote Work and Its Hidden Costs
passages.passage:
Five years ago, working from home was a privilege offered to a small number of employees. Today, it is normal for entire teams to meet only through video calls. The shift began during the global pandemic, but it has continued long after offices reopened. Many workers say they would resign rather than return full time to a traditional office.

The benefits are clear. Without commuting, people save money on transportation and food. Parents can pick up children from school without missing meetings. Workers in expensive cities can move to smaller towns where housing is more affordable. Companies, in turn, can hire talented people from anywhere in the world, which used to be much harder.

However, remote work has hidden costs that are only now becoming visible. New employees often struggle to build relationships with colleagues they have never met in person. Casual conversations in the office, which once led to creative ideas, no longer happen as easily. Managers report that it is harder to evaluate junior staff fairly when most of the work is done in private. Some studies suggest that fully remote workers are promoted less often than those who appear in the office regularly.

Mental health is another concern. While working from home gives flexibility, it also blurs the line between work and personal life. Without the routine of leaving the office, many employees end up working longer hours and feeling that they are always available. Loneliness has become a real problem, especially for those who live alone and rarely meet colleagues face to face.

In response, many companies are experimenting with hybrid arrangements. Employees might work from home three days a week and come to the office for the other two. This approach attempts to keep the flexibility that workers value while preserving the human connections that fully remote work tends to weaken. It is not a perfect solution, and it is still being adjusted in real time.

The long-term picture is unclear. Remote work has changed expectations forever, but the right balance between home and office is still being worked out. The companies that find that balance first will likely gain a competitive advantage in attracting and keeping the people they need most.

passages.title: What Modern Science Tells Us About Sleep
passages.passage:
Everyone sleeps, but few people think about why. For most of history, sleep was a mystery. Some cultures believed that the soul left the body during sleep. Others thought sleep was wasted time that could be reduced with the right diet or willpower. Modern science has finally begun to explain what really happens when we close our eyes.

When you fall asleep, your brain does not switch off. Instead, it enters a complex cycle of stages. Light sleep helps the body relax. Deep sleep allows the body to repair muscles and release growth hormones. The final stage, called REM sleep, is when most dreams happen. During REM, the brain is almost as active as when you are awake, but the body is paralyzed so you do not act out your dreams.

Each stage plays a different role. Deep sleep is important for the physical body. REM sleep, on the other hand, is now believed to help with memory and emotional health. If you study a list of English words and then sleep well, your brain will organize what you learned overnight. The next day, you will remember more than someone who stayed up all night studying.

When sleep is short or interrupted, the consequences are real. People who sleep less than six hours a night for many days show slower reaction times and worse decision-making, similar to mild alcohol intoxication. Long-term lack of sleep is linked to weight gain, depression, and heart disease. In short, your bed is not a place where time is wasted. It is one of the most important medical tools you own — and it costs nothing to use.

The simplest advice from researchers is also the hardest to follow: go to bed at the same time every night, keep the room cool and dark, and put your phone in another room.

passages.title: Will Artificial Intelligence Take Our Jobs?
passages.passage:
Every major technological revolution in history has caused two things at the same time: it has eliminated certain kinds of work and it has created new kinds. The arrival of the steam engine, electricity, and personal computers each followed this pattern. Many of the jobs people perform today did not exist a hundred years ago. The current debate about artificial intelligence is asking whether AI will follow the same path or break it.

Unlike previous technologies, AI does not simply automate physical labor. It is increasingly capable of tasks that were once considered uniquely human: writing reports, analyzing legal documents, designing visuals, and even producing music. A growing number of office workers, including those with university degrees, are watching tools that can do parts of their job in seconds. For some, this is convenient. For others, it raises serious questions about whether their skills will still be valued in five or ten years.

Economists who study these shifts tend to be cautiously optimistic. They argue that AI will reshape work rather than destroy it. Routine cognitive tasks — writing standard emails, summarizing meetings, producing first drafts — may be handled by software. But the tasks that remain will likely involve judgment, communication, persuasion, and the ability to coordinate with other people. Those skills may become more valuable, not less.

However, the transition is unlikely to be smooth. Workers in industries that are hit first will face real pressure to retrain. The people most affected are not usually the engineers who build the tools, but ordinary professionals — translators, junior accountants, content writers, customer support staff. Without intentional policy support, the gap between people who adapt and people who do not could widen quickly.

There is also a deeper question that economists rarely answer directly: even if new jobs are created, will there be enough of them, and will workers be able to move into them in time? History suggests it is possible, but the transition periods can last decades. During those periods, many individuals are left behind, even as overall productivity rises.

For students and young professionals, the practical advice is consistent across experts. Learn to use AI tools well — they are tools, not enemies. Develop skills that are hard to automate: deep technical expertise, creative problem solving, and the human side of work that depends on trust and judgment. Stay curious, because the most valuable skills five years from now may not yet have a name.

The history of technology suggests that AI alone will not cause a permanent crisis of work. But it also suggests that pretending nothing will change is a poor strategy. The people who do best are usually not those who fear the future or those who deny it, but those who study it carefully and prepare.

passages.title: Street Food: The Taste of Everyday Vietnam
passages.passage:
Walk down almost any street in Vietnam in the early morning and you will smell something delicious. Women sell sticky rice from baskets, men fry bread on small stoves, and steam rises from huge pots of broth. For millions of people, breakfast does not happen at home. It happens on a tiny plastic stool at the side of the road.

Street food is popular for three simple reasons. First, it is cheap. A bowl of noodle soup or a banh mi often costs less than a cup of coffee in a modern cafe. Second, it is fast. Office workers and students can eat in ten minutes and still arrive on time. Third, and most important, it tastes good. Many sellers cook only one dish, and they have made it the same way for years, sometimes for decades.

Each region has its own favorites. In Hanoi, people love pho and bun cha, grilled pork served with cold rice noodles and fresh herbs. In Hue, the most famous dish is bun bo, a spicy beef noodle soup. In Ho Chi Minh City, you can find com tam, or broken rice, served with grilled pork and a fried egg. Travelers often say that the best way to understand a city is to eat what the local people eat.

Street food is also changing. Some customers worry about hygiene, so many sellers now wear gloves and keep their food in clean, covered containers. Young people order street food through delivery apps, and some popular stalls have become famous on social media. A few even appear in international food guides.

Still, the heart of street food stays the same. It is about sitting close to strangers, chatting with the seller, and enjoying a simple meal together. For many Vietnamese people living abroad, the thing they miss most is not a fancy restaurant. It is a hot bowl of soup on a busy street corner at seven in the morning.

passages.title: Tet: More Than a New Year Holiday
passages.passage:
Tet, the Lunar New Year, is the most important holiday in Vietnam. It usually falls in late January or February. For about a week, offices close, streets become quiet, and millions of people travel back to their hometowns. Train and bus tickets often sell out weeks before the holiday.

Preparation starts early. Families clean their houses from top to bottom, because people believe cleaning sweeps away the bad luck of the old year. They buy peach blossoms in the north or yellow apricot blossoms in the south to decorate their homes. Many families also make banh chung, a square cake of sticky rice, green beans, and pork, wrapped in green leaves and boiled for many hours.

The first days of the new year are full of customs. People visit relatives, wear new clothes, and say kind wishes such as "good health" and "success." Children receive lucky money in small red envelopes from adults. Many people believe that the first visitor to enter a house after midnight decides the family's luck for the whole year, so some families carefully choose a kind, successful friend to be that person.

Today, Tet is changing in some ways. Busy young people often buy banh chung instead of making it. Some families choose to travel to the beach or abroad during the holiday instead of staying at home. Lucky money can now be sent by bank transfer or e-wallet, which some older people find a little strange.

However, the main meaning of Tet has not changed. It is a time to rest after a long year, to remember family members who have passed away, and to be together. For many workers who live far from home, the long trip back is tiring, but they say it is worth it. No matter where they are, they want to be home for Tet.

passages.title: Small Steps to Save Money
passages.passage:
Linh is a 22-year-old university student in Da Nang. Last year, she had a part-time job at a bookshop, but at the end of every month her wallet was empty. "I didn't buy anything expensive," she says. "I just didn't know where my money went." Many young people have the same problem.

Linh decided to write down everything she spent for one month. The result surprised her. She spent almost a quarter of her income on milk tea and snacks. She also paid for two music and video subscriptions that she rarely used, and she often ordered food through apps late at night because she was too tired to cook.

She made a few simple changes. First, she made a budget. When she got her salary, she divided it into three parts: money for needs like rent and food, money for wants like coffee with friends, and money for savings. Second, she cancelled the subscriptions she did not use. Third, she started cooking simple meals on Sunday for the next few days.

Linh did not stop having fun. She still meets her friends for milk tea, but now it is once a week, not every day. She also uses a savings app that automatically moves a small amount of money into a separate account. "If I can't see the money, I don't spend it," she laughs.

After six months, Linh had saved enough money to buy a second-hand laptop for her studies. More importantly, she felt calmer. She no longer worried at the end of each month. Her message to other students is simple: you don't need to earn a lot to save. You just need to know where your money goes and make small changes every day.

passages.title: Selling Live: How Livestream Shopping Changed Online Retail
passages.passage:
On a weekday evening, thousands of people in Vietnam are watching the same thing on their phones: a young woman holding up a jar of face cream, talking quickly and laughing with viewers. Every few seconds, a new comment appears asking about the price or the size. Within an hour, she has sold several hundred jars. This is livestream shopping, and in just a few years it has become one of the fastest-growing ways to buy and sell goods.

The idea is simple. A seller broadcasts live video on a platform such as TikTok, Facebook, or Shopee, shows the products, and answers questions in real time. Viewers can tap a button to buy without leaving the stream. Unlike a traditional online store, where customers look at photos and read descriptions alone, a livestream feels social and personal. Buyers can ask the seller to try on a shirt or test a product in front of the camera.

For small businesses, the benefits are clear. A farmer selling dried mangoes or a family running a clothing shop no longer needs an expensive storefront on a busy street. All they need is a phone, good lighting, and the confidence to talk to strangers. Some sellers have built large audiences and now earn more than they ever did from a physical shop.

However, the boom has also created problems. Because sales happen so fast, some sellers exaggerate the quality of their products or even sell fake goods. Customers who buy on impulse may regret it when the package arrives. Tax authorities have also struggled to keep track of income from thousands of individual sellers, and new rules now make platforms more responsible for reporting what their sellers earn.

Experts believe livestream shopping is here to stay, but it will probably become more professional. Large brands are hiring trained hosts, and platforms are investing in tools to check product quality and handle complaints. For buyers, the best advice remains the same as with any kind of shopping: compare prices, read reviews, and never let the excitement of a countdown timer make the decision for you.

passages.title: The Plastic in Our Daily Lives
passages.passage:
Think about the last time you bought a drink from a street vendor. It probably came in a plastic cup with a plastic lid, a plastic straw, and a thin plastic bag to carry it. You used all of these for perhaps fifteen minutes. The plastic, however, could stay in the environment for hundreds of years.

Vietnam, like many fast-growing countries in Asia, uses a large amount of single-use plastic. As incomes have risen, people buy more packaged food, order more takeaway, and shop more online, and almost every one of these habits creates plastic waste. Much of this waste is never recycled. It ends up in landfills, is burned in the open air, or is carried by rivers into the sea, where it harms fish, turtles, and seabirds.

The problem is not only about animals. Over time, plastic breaks down into tiny pieces called microplastics. Scientists have found these particles in tap water, sea salt, and seafood. Researchers are still studying how microplastics affect human health, but many are concerned that they could carry harmful chemicals into our bodies.

There are signs of change. Several supermarkets have started wrapping vegetables in banana leaves instead of plastic film, an idea that attracted attention around the world. Some cafes offer a discount to customers who bring their own cups, and paper or rice straws are increasingly common. The government has also set targets to reduce single-use plastic bags and other plastic products in shops and tourist areas.

Individual actions may seem small, but they add up. Carrying a reusable bottle, saying "no straw, please," or bringing a cloth bag to the market costs almost nothing. Real progress, however, also requires better recycling systems and companies that design packaging with the environment in mind. Plastic is cheap and convenient, and that is exactly why reducing it takes effort from everyone, not just from a few enthusiastic individuals.

vocabulary.meaning: người bán hàng (thường là hàng rong)
vocabulary.example: A fruit vendor stands outside my school every afternoon.

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3 says researchers are still studying the effects, but many are concerned they could carry harmful chemicals into our bodies.

options: Burning plastic waste in the open air

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4 says supermarkets wrapping vegetables in banana leaves was an idea that attracted attention around the world.

options: Individual actions are useless

quiz.explanation: The last paragraph says individual actions add up, but real progress also requires better recycling systems and companies designing packaging with the environment in mind.

passages.title: The Attention Economy: Why Short Videos Are So Hard to Stop Watching
passages.passage:
Many people have had the same experience: you open an app to check one message, and forty minutes later you are still scrolling through short videos, unable to remember most of what you watched. It is tempting to blame a lack of self-control. Yet this behavior is less a personal failing than the predictable result of products deliberately engineered to capture as much of our attention as possible.

The business logic is straightforward. Most social media platforms are free to use, and they earn money by selling advertising. The longer users stay, the more ads they see and the more data the company collects about their preferences. In this model, often called the attention economy, the user's time and focus are effectively the product being sold.

To keep people watching, designers rely on well-understood psychological principles. The endless feed removes natural stopping points, so there is never a moment when the content simply ends. Recommendation algorithms learn within minutes which topics hold a particular user's interest. Most powerfully, the unpredictability of what comes next, a dull clip followed perhaps by a hilarious one, works much like a slot machine, encouraging users to keep swiping in search of the next reward.

The consequences are still debated. Some studies link heavy social media use, particularly among teenagers, to anxiety, poor sleep, and difficulty concentrating on demanding tasks such as reading a long text. Other researchers caution that the evidence is mixed and that correlation does not prove causation: anxious people may simply spend more time online. What few dispute is that time spent scrolling is time not spent on sleep, exercise, or face-to-face conversation.

Regulators have begun to respond. Some countries now require platforms to offer young users screen-time limits, restrict notifications at night, or give people the option of seeing content in chronological order rather than through an algorithm. Critics argue that such measures place the burden on individuals rather than challenging the underlying business model.

In the meantime, people are developing their own strategies. Some turn off non-essential notifications or switch their phone screen to grayscale, which makes apps less visually appealing. Others set aside phone-free hours or delete the most absorbing apps entirely. None of these approaches is perfect, but they share a common insight: in a contest between one person's willpower and a team of engineers optimizing for engagement, it helps to change the environment rather than rely on discipline alone.

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the unpredictability of what comes next works like a slot machine, encouraging users to keep swiping in search of the next reward.

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains the caution with the example that anxious people may simply spend more time online, so the link may not be cause and effect.

options: They are too expensive for governments

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 5 says critics argue the measures place the burden on individuals rather than challenging the underlying business model.

options: Willpower alone is usually enough

quiz.explanation: The last paragraph concludes that, against engineers optimizing for engagement, it helps to change the environment rather than rely on discipline alone.

passages.title: Can Vietnam’s Cities Move Beyond the Motorbike?
passages.passage:
For visitors arriving in Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City for the first time, the most striking sight is often the traffic: a seemingly endless river of motorbikes flowing through intersections, carrying everything from schoolchildren to refrigerators. With tens of millions of motorbikes registered nationwide, the two-wheeler is not merely a vehicle in Vietnam; it is the backbone of daily life.

The motorbike's dominance is easy to explain. It is affordable, far cheaper than a car, and perfectly suited to narrow alleys that cars cannot enter. It allows a single person to commute, run a small business, and transport a family. For decades, public transport in Vietnamese cities consisted mainly of buses that were slow and stuck in the same traffic as everyone else, so there was little reason to give up the freedom of two wheels.

Yet this model is reaching its limits. Rush-hour congestion costs the cities enormous amounts of lost time and productivity. Air pollution in Hanoi regularly reaches levels considered unhealthy, especially in winter, and vehicle exhaust is a major contributor. Meanwhile, the rapid growth in private cars is making the situation worse, since a single car occupies the road space of several motorbikes.

City authorities have responded with a mixture of investment and restriction. Both major cities have opened their first urban railway lines after years of delays, and further lines are planned. Hanoi has also announced plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorbikes in its central districts, encouraging a shift toward electric vehicles and public transport.

Such policies face real obstacles. Millions of people, including street vendors and delivery drivers, depend on motorbikes for their income, and restricting them without reliable alternatives could hurt the poorest residents most. Metro lines also work well only when people can reach the stations easily, which requires safe sidewalks, feeder buses, and shaded walkways, infrastructure that many neighborhoods still lack.

The experience of other Asian cities suggests that change is possible but gradual. Taipei, which also has a strong scooter culture, built an extensive metro network and combined it with reliable buses and more walkable streets, gradually persuading many residents to leave their scooters at home for daily commutes. For Vietnam, the challenge is to make public transport so convenient that people choose it willingly, rather than forcing them off their motorbikes before a genuine alternative exists.

passages.title: Brain Drain or Brain Gain? The Debate Over Studying Abroad
passages.passage:
Every year, tens of thousands of young Vietnamese leave the country to study at universities in Australia, Japan, South Korea, the United States, and Europe. Vietnam has become one of the largest sources of international students in the world. For many families, sending a child abroad represents years of savings and sacrifice, driven by the belief that a foreign degree opens doors that would otherwise remain closed.

Supporters of studying abroad point to clear benefits. Students gain fluency in a foreign language, exposure to different teaching methods, and the kind of independence that comes from managing life in an unfamiliar country. Many universities abroad emphasize critical thinking and class discussion over memorization, which graduates say changes the way they approach problems.

The concern, often called "brain drain," is that many of the most talented students never come back. Higher salaries, better research facilities, and, for some, a preference for a different lifestyle encourage graduates to build careers overseas. When a country invests in educating its brightest young people only to see them contribute to another economy, the loss can be significant, particularly in fields such as medicine, engineering, and scientific research.

Recent thinking, however, suggests the picture is more complicated. Economists increasingly speak of "brain circulation" rather than a one-way drain. Vietnamese professionals working abroad send money home, invest in local start-ups, and connect Vietnamese companies with international partners. Some return after a decade with not only skills but also networks and capital that would have been impossible to acquire at home. Vietnam's growing technology sector owes a good deal to such returnees.

Whether graduates come back often depends less on patriotism than on practical conditions. Returnees frequently mention obstacles such as lower pay, rigid workplace hierarchies, and difficulty getting foreign qualifications recognized. Conversely, a dynamic job market, competitive research funding, and a sense that their ideas will be taken seriously can make returning an attractive choice.

For students considering an overseas degree, the decision is ultimately personal and financial, and it deserves careful thought. A foreign diploma is no longer the guaranteed advantage it once was, as Vietnamese universities improve and employers increasingly value practical skills. Yet for those who go with clear goals, the experience can offer something that is difficult to measure: the ability to see their own country, and its possibilities, through fresh eyes.

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the loss comes when a country educates its brightest young people only to see them contribute to another economy, especially in medicine, engineering, and research.

options: Talented people should never leave their home country

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that professionals abroad send money home, invest in start-ups, connect companies with partners, and sometimes return with skills, networks, and capital.

options: Their sense of patriotism

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 5 says returning depends less on patriotism than on practical conditions like pay, rigid hierarchies, recognition of qualifications, and job market dynamism.

options: Because foreign universities have become easier

quiz.explanation: The last paragraph gives two reasons: Vietnamese universities are improving and employers increasingly value practical skills.

What could Vietnamese companies and universities do to attract talented returnees?
